claim: About 66% of long-duration USOS crew members show at least one early sign of SANS: optic disc edema 64%, chorioretinal folds 15%, globe flattening 26%, hyperopic shift of +0.75 D or more 14%.
nNote: Cohort size not stated in the report.
effect: 66% with at least one early sign
limitations: Prevalence of signs, not of functional vision loss.

claim: NASA clinical criteria: an increase of 20 um or more in total peripapillary retinal thickness is an early indication of optic disc edema; 55 um or more and/or Frisen grade 1 or higher is clinically concerning.
nNote: Clinical criterion, not a sample estimate.
effect: Delta TRT >= 20 um early; >= 55 um and/or Frisen >= 1 concerning
limitations: These are SANS clinical criteria; they do not come from Standard Measures.

claim: VaPER bed-rest analog (30 days at -6 degrees head-down tilt with 0.5% CO2): each hour of total sleep below the mean was associated with higher odds of optic disc edema.
effect: OR 2.2 per hour of sleep below the mean
limitations: Association in a small analog; it does not show causation in astronauts.

claim: VaPER: each 0.1 C decrease in circadian temperature amplitude was associated with higher odds of optic disc edema (OR 4.0). Also NREM stage 2 sleep OR 4.8 [1.3-18.6] and wake after sleep onset OR 3.6 [1.2-10.6].
effect: OR 4.0 per -0.1 C of circadian amplitude
limitations: Wide intervals from 11 subjects.

claim: Lower body negative pressure (about -25 mmHg, 3 h twice daily, bed-rest substudy) gave intracranial responses similar to seated posture; efficacy against SANS is not established and the HRR gap stays open.
limitations: The publication itself says conclusions need the control group. LBNP must not be labeled a validated SANS treatment.

claim: ISS reference cohort: bone mineral density fell about 0.8 +/- 0.5 %/month at the lumbar spine, 1.1 +/- 0.5 at the femoral neck and 1.2 +/- 0.9 at the trochanter (DXA); trabecular loss at the femoral neck reached 2.7 +/- 1.9 %/month (QCT).
limitations: Historical cohort; large spread between individuals.

claim: After the move from iRED to ARED, mean monthly bone loss fell from about 1.0 %/month (24 iRED users) to 0.3-0.5 %/month (11 ARED users).
limitations: Observational comparison between eras, not a randomized trial.

claim: Alendronate 70 mg weekly plus exercise (treated astronauts vs 14 historical ISS controls): femoral neck -1.1 +/- 0.5 to -0.2 +/- 0.3 %/month (DXA); trabecular femoral neck -2.7 +/- 1.9 to -0.2 +/- 0.8 %/month (QCT).
limitations: Very small sample and high variability. It supports monitoring adherence and response; it does not authorize starting a bisphosphonate without a pre-approved medical protocol.

claim: ISS data: calf volume fell 10-16% and thigh volume 4-7%; knee strength fell 10.4-24.1% and ankle strength 4-22.3%.
nNote: Cohort size not stated in the report.
limitations: Measured with the exercise hardware of that era.

claim: Exercise countermeasures reduce but do not eliminate losses; some astronauts keep 10-15% deficits.
limitations: Exploration vehicles may carry less capable exercise hardware.

claim: Orthostatic intolerance affects about 30% of crew after short flights (4-18 days) and up to 83% after long-duration flights.
effect: about 30% short flights; up to 83% long flights
limitations: Measured on return to gravity.

claim: Salt and water loading reduced the heart-rate response to orthostatic stress by about 29% (17 treated vs 9 untreated astronauts).
limitations: Non-randomized series.

claim: Compression garments (7 treated vs 7 control Shuttle astronauts): heart-rate rise on standing 11 +/- 1 vs 21 +/- 4 bpm; systolic pressure change +2 +/- 4 vs -9 +/- 2 mmHg.
effect: heart-rate rise 11 vs 21 bpm; systolic +2 vs -9 mmHg
limitations: Short Shuttle flights; 7 per group.

claim: Four hours of LBNP at -30 mmHg with fluid loading (13 Shuttle astronauts) restored heart-rate and blood-pressure responses the next day; the effect was gone by the second day.
effect: response restored for one day only
limitations: Temporary effect.

claim: NASA-STD-3001 Vol. 2 [V2 6004]: the one-hour average partial pressure of CO2 shall be 3 mmHg or less. Off-nominal limits are defined per program or project.
limitations: The standard gives no universal table of yellow and red alerts.

claim: ISS Expeditions 2-31: 19 of 49 astronauts (about 38.7%) reported headache; the odds of headache roughly doubled for each 1 mmHg increase in CO2. A 7-day average below 2.5 mmHg corresponds to an estimated risk under 1%; 3 mmHg to about 1.4%.
effect: odds ratio about 2 per +1 mmHg of CO2
limitations: Epidemiological association from self-reported headache; 2.5 mmHg is not a NASA red limit.

claim: VaPER exposed 11 bed-rest subjects to 0.5% CO2 (about 4 mmHg) for 30 days.
limitations: Ground analog.

claim: Shuttle study of 17 astronauts: 14 shed Epstein-Barr virus in saliva; EBV was found in 21% of samples and VZV in 7.4%, against about 3% and under 1% in healthy controls.
effect: EBV in 21% of samples vs about 3% in controls
limitations: Percentages of samples, not of people.

claim: Long-duration series: VZV reactivated in about 50% of astronauts; CMV was present in 35% of in-flight urine samples.
limitations: One figure counts people and the other counts samples; they are not comparable.

claim: There is no universal preventive pharmacological countermeasure for immune changes; HRR gap IM-106 on the combined effect of hazards remains open.
limitations: Hypothesis level.

claim: Standard Measures, 19 ISS crew members, 2,137 in-flight nights (2019-2022): sleep 7.33 +/- 1.16 h in flight vs 7.87 +/- 1.10 h before and 7.75 +/- 1.43 h after flight.
limitations: Sleep loss is not inevitable: risk must be judged against the individual baseline and trend.

claim: Cognition in astronauts and analogs (baseline n=97; 48 in 45-day and 34 in 4-8-month analogs): after correction for multiple comparisons, only sensorimotor function differed between long and short duration.
limitations: Pools several analogs; it is not a HERA-only result.

claim: The Psychomotor Vigilance Test is validated as a fatigue measure on the ISS, but there is no validated universal NASA alert threshold (HRR gap BMed-102).
limitations: No published limit of the form 'reaction time above N ms is red'.

claim: MSL/RAD measured about 1.84 mSv/day during the cruise to Mars. This is an observed environment rate, not an alert threshold.
limitations: Depends on solar cycle and shielding of that spacecraft.

claim: MSL/RAD measured about 0.7 mSv/day on the Martian surface. This is an observed environment rate, not an alert threshold.
limitations: Conditions at Gale crater during the measurement period.

claim: Artemis I: operational estimate of 22.3 mSv mean effective dose for a hypothetical male crew member over the mission.
nNote: Model estimate for a hypothetical crew member.
limitations: Uncrewed flight; computed, not worn dosimetry.

claim: Water or polyethylene shielding gives about 50% average dose reduction for solar particle events but only about 7% for galactic cosmic rays.
effect: about -50% for SPE, about -7% for GCR
limitations: Depends on thickness and architecture.

claim: MARE on Artemis I: the AstroRad vest reduced effective dose in the inner-belt transit by about 25.8 +/- 0.4%; models project 58.2% for an August 1972-type event and 36.9% for an October 1989-type event.
effect: -25.8% measured in belt transit; -58.2% and -36.9% modeled for historical events
limitations: The two event figures are model extrapolations: Artemis I crossed no event of that size.

claim: NASA-STD-3001 Vol. 1 sets radiation limits per mission and career. It publishes no yellow or red limit for daily dose rate.
limitations: An instantaneous rate must not be turned into a medical diagnosis.

claim: Integrated Medical Model example scenario, expected events per simulated mission: late insomnia 13.85, skin abrasion 9.86, skin rash 9.83, late headache 5.25, nasal congestion 3.51, respiratory infection 3.46, CO2 headache 2.15, SANS 2.08.
limitations: Expected events per simulated mission, not observed prevalence. They depend on mission length and crew size and must not be converted to percentages.

claim: IMM validation under-predicted Shuttle conditions by about 10% and over-predicted ISS conditions by about 20%.
limitations: Baselined for the ISS; exploration use needs care.

claim: NASA's Autonomous Medical Operations project defines an onboard medical decision support system that assists, and does not replace, the Crew Medical Officer; ExMC gap Medical-101 remains open.
effect: NR: no published overall clinical efficacy
limitations: Decision support, not diagnosis.

claim: NASA's Human Research Program lists inadequate food and nutrition as a risk of long missions: stored food loses nutrients and crews often eat less than they need. No alert threshold is published.
limitations: Not part of the research report matrix; added so that the nutrition indicators carry a provenance.

claim: The Lunar Lander Neutrons and Dosimetry experiment on Chang'E-4 measured about 1.37 mSv/day on the lunar surface. This is an observed environment rate, not an alert threshold.
effect: about 1.37 mSv/day on the lunar surface
limitations: Not in the research report; it is the simulator's lunar environment parameter.

claim: Typical crew exposure on the International Space Station is roughly 0.5 to 0.7 mSv/day. This is an environment rate, not an alert threshold.
limitations: Not in the research report and no source located yet: it is the simulator's station environment parameter and must not be cited as verified.
